title: Britain after 1947
hookLine: Sikhs settle in Southall, Birmingham and the mill towns, building gurdwaras in old houses

lines: SHOES PILED BY ONE FRONT STEP.
cards: A row of narrow brick houses in an English town, the 1960s. Every house the same: a front door, a bay window, a little back yard. But on a Sunday morning, one of them is different.
Shoes are piled by the front step. Men with covered heads and women in bright scarves go in and out.
Through the window comes singing and the beat of a tabla, and from the back, the smell of dal and rotis cooking for everyone who comes.

teach.b: After the Second World War, Britain was short of workers; its factories, foundries and mills needed hands. And after Partition, many Punjabi families had lost land and needed a new start.
So from the 1950s Sikh men came, often one from a village first, then his brothers and cousins.

They worked in the foundries of Birmingham and the West Midlands, the textile mills of Yorkshire and Lancashire, and the factories and airport near Southall in west London. They shared crowded houses to save money.

In the 1960s, wives and children joined them; later, more Sikh families came from Kenya and Uganda. London had had a gurdwara since before the First World War, but most of these new towns had nothing.
So Sikhs did what they had done in Hong Kong and California: they bought an ordinary house.

teach.h: THE GURU IN THE FRONT ROOM.
teach.b: The front room, sometimes knocked through into the next, became the darbar: the Guru Granth Sahib on a raised seat under a canopy, the sangat on the carpet before it. The kitchen made langar.
Every morning someone performed the parkash, opening the Guru for the day, and every evening laid it to rest.
A house became a gurdwara. As the community grew, they bought old churches, cinemas and factories, and eventually built large gurdwaras of their own.
But many British Sikh families still talk about that first house: the shoes on the step, the carpet in the front room, langar from a terraced kitchen.

how: In Britain, many gurdwaras began in terraced houses, and later in converted churches, cinemas and factories; each morning the Guru Granth Sahib is opened (parkash) and each night it is laid to rest.

games.q: Sikhs in Britain — tap the pairs.

games.q: it's the 1960s, and your community has bought a terraced house to be its gurdwara. where does the Guru Granth Sahib go?
o: in a cupboard, until a proper building is ready.
in the front room, on a raised seat, with the sangat before it.
in the kitchen, beside the langar.
games.why: the front room became the darbar: the Guru on a raised seat, opened each morning and laid to rest each night, with the sangat before it.

practice: Picture a building you pass often without thinking, an old shop, a house, a hall on your street, and wonder who might have gathered there, and what was sung, cooked, prayed or celebrated inside.
Let its ordinary walls fill with people and stories. Then think of your own home, and what makes it sacred to someone.

wordCard.voice: Parkash. The morning ceremony of opening the Guru Granth Sahib — performed in the houses Sikhs turned into gurdwaras after coming to Britain's foundries, mills and factories from 1947.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: parkash, light; the morning ceremony of opening the Guru Granth Sahib.
